title: I Let the Community-Lathe Tailstock Clock Catch the Mentor Who Camped My Centers

parts.text: I stepped into lathe three at 10:05 a.m. and mentor Holt was already using my numbered centers. The board said: NINETY MINUTES. CENTERS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-nine, woodshop steward, holding a clipboard that listed our blank. Holt shrugged. "Mentors keep the spindle." I photographed the board, the booking, and his blank on my centers. Then I asked for the tailstock clock. At 10:13 the shop desk pinged why Holt's blank sat on our centers. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The shop desk can see Holt's blank on lathe three during our ninety minutes.

social.video_title: He camped my numbered lathe centers — Part 1/2
social.description: Community lathe, a mentor on my centers, a ninety-minute clock he posted. I logged the blank. Would you have asked for the tailstock clock?

parts.text: Holt called it roughing until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the tailstock still. The centers went back to my numbered tray. Holt ran a slot of their own and told the next mentor atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: MENTORS DO NOT KEEP THE SPINDLE. I keep our blank on a labeled card. Holt brown-bags his blanks. The lathe finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Mentors do not keep the spindle — Part 2/2
social.description: Tailstock clock, numbered centers, and a second line on the board. Was roughing ever our ninety minutes?
